items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the family court act, in relation to probation in child support, juvenile delinquency, persons in need of supervision and family offense proceedings
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:S7589

TITLE OF BILL:
An act
to amend the family court act, in relation to probation in child
support, juvenile delinquency, persons in need of supervision and family
offense proceedings

This is one in a series of measures being introduced at the request of
the Chief Administrative Judge upon the recommendation of her Family
Court Advisory and Rules Committee.

Chapter 97 of the Laws of 2011 made far-reaching changes to the
provisions of Family Court Act § 176 regarding orders of probation in
family offense, child support, juvenile delinquency (JD) and persons
in need of supervision (PINS) proceedings.
Section 176, originally enacted in 1933 and incorporated into the
Family Court Act in 1962, had "(t)hrough almost eighty years of
experience...proven useful and uncontroversial." Sobie, Practice
Commentaries, Family Court Act § 176 (McKinney's, 2011).
Unfortunately, the changes made by chapter 97 have created
significant controversy. They contradict other venue provisions of
the Family Court Act and have imposed substantial burdens upon adults
and juveniles subject to orders of probation, as well as upon the
Family Court. This measure is designed to ameliorate these problems.

First, as to JD and PINS cases in which the youth resides in a
jurisdiction other than that in which probation had been ordered, the
measure amends Family Court Act § 176(1) to require the court to
transfer probation supervision to the probation department in the
jurisdiction of the probationer's residence, including in cases in
which the probationer's relocation occurs subsequent to issuance of
an order of probation. In other cases involving orders of probation,
the court would have discretion to transfer probation supervision to
the jurisdiction in which the probationer resides. Importantly, the
measure eliminates the provision in the 2011 statute that placed
responsibility upon probationers, whether adult or juvenile, to
request permission from the court to relocate their residences and
gave the court authority to rule upon such requests. That provision
is over-broad in the context of an adult probationer in a child
support or family offense case and is particularly inappropriate when
applied to a JD or PINS case, where the probationer's parents, not
the juvenile probationer, control decisions regarding where the
family resides.

Second, the measure amends sections 171 and 175 of the Family Court
Act to indicate that its provisions regarding venue for all
proceedings to enforce or modify Family Court orders, including
proceedings for violations of probation, do not apply to
probation-related proceedings involving juveniles in PINS and JD
proceedings.

Proceedings involving juveniles placed on probation in such cases
would instead be governed by Family Court Act §176(2). That section
is amended to provide that a transfer of probation supervision to the
jurisdiction in which the probationer resides creates a rebuttable
presumption that subsequent proceedings regarding the probation
order, including proceedings for a probation violation or proceedings
to extend the duration or modify the conditions of probation, should
be heard in the county providing the supervision. The presumption
would be rebutted if Family Court in the jurisdiction providing the
supervision "determines that there is a good cause to return the
proceeding" to the court that issued the order of probation. '

Significantly, the presumption would not apply to the wide range of
other post-dispositional proceedings in JD and PINS proceedings that
are unrelated to the order of probation, since petitioners and the
Family Courts in such cases retain discretion to exercise other venue
options. See, e.g., Family Court Act §§355.1, 761,762, 780. Family
Court Act § 174 provides that Family Court, upon good cause, may
transfer venue to any county in which a proceeding may have been
filed and must transfer venue if it had been improperly lodged. This
measure thus resolves the conflicting venue provisions by applying
the presumption in favor of the probationer's county of residence
only to those JD and PINS proceedings that pertain directly to the
order of probation.

In limiting transfer of Family Court proceedings in JD and PINS cases
to those related specifically to the order of probation, the measure
would conform the statutory language to the construction given by the
Court of Appeals to analogous language applicable to
post-dispositional criminal proceedings. CPL §410.80(2), upon which
the 2011 amendments to Family Court Act § 176 were based, provides
that once probation supervision over a criminal defendant has been
transferred, the court in the probationer's county of residence
"shall assume all powers and duties of the sentencing court and shall
have sole jurisdiction in the case..." However, the Court of Appeals
held, in People v. Mitchell, 15 N.Y.3d 93 (2010), that, although
the phrase "sole jurisdiction" appears to
divest the sentencing court of jurisdiction over all
post-dispositional proceedings, the Legislature simply intended to
transfer "the full range of powers and duties necessary for the
Judiciary to carry out its responsibilities to enforce the terms and
conditions of probationers, and to deal with forfeitures and
disabilities," but did not intend to deprive the sentencing court of
jurisdiction to rule upon post-judgment motions under Article 440 of
the CPL.

Moreover, in limiting the presumptive transfer provision to JD and
PINS cases, the measure leaves intact the venue provisions applicable
in family offense and child support cases. Family Court Act §818, for
example, provides that a petitioner in a family offense case may file
in the county where the offense allegedly occurred or in any county
where any of the parties reside, which may include a domestic

violence shelter to which a petitioner has fled for safety. Venue in
child support proceedings, pursuant to Family Court Act §419, may be
in any county in which a party resides and may be transferred by
Family Court, upon application, in accordance with CPLR article five.

Third, the measure eliminates an unnecessary burden and unfunded
mandate imposed upon Family Courts by the court records transfer
provisions of chapter 97 of the Laws of 2011. That statute requires
Family Courts to transfer all court records immediately upon a
transfer of probation supervision, even when there has been no
probation violation or other probation-related post-dispositional
proceeding pending in the county that is providing probation
supervision and even when the records may include years of litigation
entirely unrelated to the order of probation. In order to limit court
records transfer requirements to those records that are necessary for
actual proceedings, the measure amends Family Court Act § 173 to
provide that where an action, including, inter alia, an action to
modify, extend or enforce an order of probation, has been filed in a
county other than the county that issued the order, Family Court in
the county in which the action has been filed must request the record
from the court that issued the order and that court must transmit a
copy of the record that pertains to the order of probation forthwith
"by electronic or other means." The measure thus targets only the
particular records that would be relevant to
the pending proceeding, requires transmittal only at such time as the
records are actually needed by the court and patties and recognizes
that an increasing number of Family Courts are minimizing the use of
paper records through electronic scanning.

Finally, the measure treats New York City as one jurisdiction, rather
than as five individual counties, with respect to Family Court Act
176. The City's Department of Probation covers all five counties and
is thus able to transfer probation supervision internally without
court orders. Transfers of proceedings and records within the five
courts that comprise the New York City Family Court are likewise
accomplished easily.

This measure would have no fiscal impact upon the State, and would
take effect immediately.

LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:
None. New proposal.
